title: The hook that fires, and the one that doesn't
spec: M08 · commit → diff scope → refresh → lint → publish
intro: Install the post-commit hook, watch one file change refresh exactly one concept, then meet the version that exits 0 and does nothing at all. The second one is the reason this module exists.

provenance.source: a replayed session over labs/sample-project with labs/M08-enrichment-hook/solution/ installed. The dependency lines and edge counts in step 2 are reproduced from a real run of labs/shared_tools/kg_extract.py; the gate output in step 5 is the exact output format of labs/M11-freshness-gate/solution/freshness_gate.py. Steps 2, 3 and 5 carry their own citations.

foot: Install it, then break it twice, in labs/M08-enrichment-hook/ — and keep the freshness gate from labs/M11-freshness-gate/ next to it.

steps.title: Install the loop
narrative: Three commands: make orderflow a git repo, drop the hook in, make it executable. There is nothing clever in the hook — twelve lines of sh — and the interesting part is everything it deliberately refuses to do.

No nohup. No backgrounding. No || true. No "skip if the machine is busy". Every one of those is a reasonable-looking line that converts a failed refresh into silent drift, and every one of them appears in real setups. Loud and synchronous beats quiet and detached.

One line does deserve attention: PYTHON="${ORDERFLOW_PYTHON:-python}". Hooks run with a minimal environment, outside any activated virtualenv, where python and python3 can be different installs with different packages. Pinning the interpreter is not fussiness; it is the difference between a hook that works on your machine and a hook that works.
steps.youDo: cd labs/sample-project · git init -q && git add -A && git commit -qm "baseline" · cp ../M08-enrichment-hook/solution/post-commit .git/hooks/post-commit (then chmod +x on macOS or Linux).

steps.title: One file changes, one concept refreshes
narrative: Touch services/billing/webhooks.py and commit. Read the four log lines as the four decisions they encode.

Line 1 is the whole cost model: the diff said services/billing/, the SERVICE_MAP table turned that into exactly one concept, and nothing else in the bundle was looked at. Line 2 is pass 1 done deterministically — the dependency facts come from the structural graph, not from a model, so that section cannot hallucinate. Line 3 records what the bundle learned. Line 4 is the gate.

Look closely at the refreshed block. All four edges are tagged INFERRED — bare-name resolution matched publish and verify_token to definitions by heuristic. The hook writes the provenance tag into the concept alongside the fact, so a reader can see which of these four the pipeline is confident about. It is confident about none of them, and it says so.
steps.youDo: Add a comment to services/billing/webhooks.py, git commit -am "billing: note retry intent", and watch. If nothing appears: the file must be named exactly post-commit, live in .git/hooks/, and be executable.

steps.title: Break the lint gate on purpose
narrative: A gate you have never seen fire is a decoration. Delete type: from billing-service.md, commit any code change, and watch the pipeline stop before publish.

Read the last line word by word, because it is more careful than it looks. It says the bundle was NOT published — not "not updated". By the time lint ran, the draft pass had already rewritten concept files on disk. The bundle is dirty and unpublished, which means the files sitting in your working tree right now must not be trusted or committed as they are.
That distinction is what separates a real gate from a report. A lint that warns lets a malformed bundle reach an agent. This one exits non-zero, and the hook refuses to pretend otherwise.
steps.youDo: Delete the type: line from one concept, commit any code change, then run echo $?. If it prints 0, your gate is decorative and you have just reproduced the failure M11 is about.

after.title: WHAT "NOT PUBLISHED" OBLIGES YOU TO DO

view.text: Restore the type: line and re-run before you commit the bundle. Do not reach for --no-verify or comment out the gate to get past it — the whole trust model of the bundle is the single sentence what is published passed the gate. The moment that stops being true, every agent downstream is reading text with no warranty on it, and nothing in the OKF spec will ever warn them.

steps.title: Now the hook that does nothing
narrative: Here is the same hook with three small improvements: it backgrounds the work so commits stay fast, it silences the output so the terminal stays clean, and it always exits 0 so a broken pipeline never blocks anyone. Every one of those was requested by a real teammate for a real reason.

Install it on Windows and commit. The commit succeeds. The hook exits 0. Git prints its usual summary. And nothing happens — Git for Windows' shell has no nohup, the error went to /dev/null, and exit 0 swallowed the rest.

Compare the two terminals. The failure signature of a hook that is working perfectly and a hook that is doing nothing at all is identical: a clean commit. That is the entire problem. Your team commits daily for three weeks, believes the graph updates, and is wrong.
steps.youDo: Grep your own hooks for the four words that hide failures: grep -nE 'nohup|\|\| true|/dev/null|& *$' .git/hooks/*. Every hit is a place a failure can go to die.

terminal.text:
[main 7c41ab9] billing: add fraud-check call

commit succeeded · hook exit code 0 · zero enrichment output · bundle unchanged

state.label: four documented ways a hook lies

cells: the rebuild process is never started
the hook's CODE_EXTS list falls out of sync with the extractor's, so real code files stop triggering rebuilds
the rebuild is skipped under load; the retry is "next commit", which on a quiet branch is days
the graph rebuilt fine, but the server that serves it is still holding the version it loaded at boot
a normal commit, and a correct file on disk
the artifact predates HEAD — which is measurable

view.text: Your defence cannot be "fix these four bugs" — new ones will ship, and the next one will also exit 0. Never trust a hook's exit code. All four of these mechanisms exit clean, which is why the check in the next step ignores the hook entirely and asks the artifact a question instead.

steps.title: The check that catches all four
narrative: Stop asking "did the hook run?" and start asking "is the artifact newer than the code?" That question has one mechanical answer: compare the graph's modification time against git log -1's commit time.

It is one comparison, and it catches every silent failure above, because however the rebuild died the symptom is the same — the artifact predates HEAD. Note the detail that makes it correct: it compares against commit time, not wall-clock age. A repo nobody has touched for a month with a month-old graph is perfectly fresh.

Notice also what the gate does not do. It does not repair anything. It refuses to proceed and prints the exact command that fixes it — including the reminder to restart any MCP server still holding the old graph, which is failure mechanism four. Detection and repair stay separate, so a broken repair path can never silence detection.
steps.youDo: Run it right after an empty commit — git commit --allow-empty -qm "no rebuild" then python ../M11-freshness-gate/solution/freshness_gate.py . --max-age-commits 0. If your setup cannot fail this, it is a demo that has not failed yet.

steps.title: Why it survives past Friday
narrative: One decision keeps this pipeline alive, and you already made it in step 2: scope every pass to the diff, not the repository. Everything else is style.

Run the arithmetic on a real repo. Four hundred services, forty commits a day. A full-repo pass drafts 400 concepts per commit at roughly 1.5K tokens each — around 600K tokens per commit, 24 million tokens a day. A diff-scoped pass on a typical commit touches one or two services: about 3K tokens per commit, 120K a day. Same freshness on the concepts that actually changed, for a two-hundredth of the cost.

The failure that follows from getting this wrong is not a big bill. It is that the pipeline gets switched off during its first expensive week — and a switched-off pipeline means confident staleness, which is the exact condition the whole system was built to prevent. A team that re-scans everything on every commit finds the pipeline too expensive well before their repo is large enough to need it.
steps.youDo: Before you commit to any of this, measure your own delta: run one real multi-agent task with and without the bundle and write down both token counts. That number is yours; every number below is somebody else's.

before.title: THE COST MODEL IN ONE DECISION

items.label: full-repo pass
items.note: 400 drafts × ~1.5K × 40 commits — a budget line that gets the pipeline killed

items.label: diff-scoped pass
items.note: ~2 drafts × ~1.5K × 40 commits — a rounding error, and identical freshness where it matters

after.title: AND THE NUMBER NOT TO QUOTE

view.text: You will see "up to 95% token reduction versus naive document loading" attached to this pattern. Treat it the way this course treats every headline: it is anecdotal and unvalidated at production scale, and it comes from focused, stable knowledge domains that flatter it. It plausibly indicates the direction of savings for pre-compiled context. It is not a planning input. And the prior gate still applies: if nothing agentic is consuming your bundle, you are not building a knowledge pipeline — you are maintaining a wiki nobody reads.
